cards.text: Amos, a sheepherder from Tekoa, has been bringing the LORD's judgment on nation after nation: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the Ammonites, Moab and even Judah (Amos 1:1-2:5). Now the LORD says that for three transgressions of Israel, even four, He will not revoke His judgment. I bet Israel was nodding along right up until they heard their OWN name.

cards.question: The LORD's first charge is that Israel sells the righteous for silver. What do they sell the needy for?

cards.text: Then the LORD says they trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth. That's walking over people like they're the kitchen floor, and NOBODY looks at the kitchen floor unless they drop a cookie.

cards.question: Israel tramples on the heads of the poor. What do they do to the needy?

cards.text: Then the LORD names something else they do. A man and his father have relations with the same girl.

cards.question: The LORD says what a man and his father do with the same girl profanes His holy name.

cards.text: And the LORD keeps going. In the house of their God, they drink wine obtained through fines.

cards.question: Israel also lies down beside every altar. What do they lie on?

cards.text: Then the LORD brings up the Amorite, the people in the land before Israel, tall like the cedars and as strong as the oaks. Friend, I'm a cookie stamper, and some days I LOSE a wrestling match with an oven mitt.

cards.question: Israel beat the Amorite because Israel's men were even taller and stronger.

cards.text: Not even close. The LORD says He destroyed the Amorite, fruit above and roots below, and He brought Israel up from the land of Egypt.

cards.question: After Egypt, the LORD led Israel ___ years in the wilderness, so they could take possession of the land of the Amorite.

cards.text: He also raised up prophets from their sons and Nazirites from their young men. Then the LORD asks, "Is this not true, O children of Israel?"

cards.question: Israel honors the prophets the LORD raised up and lets them prophesy.
And the Nazirites the LORD raised up? Israel made them drink ___.

cards.text: Ordering the prophets to stop prophesying is like yanking the battery out of the smoke detector: the beeping stops, but the smoke doesn't. Then the LORD says, "Behold, I am about to crush you in your place as with a cart full of grain."

cards.question: Israel has swift runners, strong men and mighty warriors. When the LORD crushes them, what does He say will fail the swift?
On that day, the fleet of foot and the horseman will at least get away.
What does the LORD say even the bravest of mighty men will do on that day?

findings.problem: Most of the stop's 11 choices are luck-based detail guesses rather than informed picks. Cards 2, 4, 8, 12, 15 and 19 ask for sandals, pushing the needy aside, garments in pledge, forty years, wine and fleeing naked without earlier cards that make those details inferable; card 6 likewise asks for an unstated next clause. A few discovery questions would be fine, but here they are the majority.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The blank is the previously unseen number "forty." Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out that number, so this tests unseen wording rather than meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The blank is the previously unseen word "wine." Card 13 only says that the LORD raised up Nazirites, and the earlier mention of wine in a different charge does not make it inferable that Israel forced the Nazirites to drink it. The blank therefore tests unseen wording rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.
